title: Houston micro-balance
as_of_note: Refining and conversion capacities as of Jan 1, 2026 (EIA Refinery Capacity Report 2026). Pipeline capacities as published by carriers and filings through Oct 2026. Flow context series: EIA PADD 2 to PADD 3 pipeline receipts Jul 2026, EIA import series 2025, Texas Gulf Coast utilization 2025 average and PADD 3 Jul 2026. Export loadings are dated vessel tracking observations from Dec 2019 and Jul 2022, not current rates.
units: kb/d unless a field name says otherwise

supply.label: Keystone and Marketlink Gulf Coast leg (South Bow)
supply.source: South Bow (owner since the Oct 1, 2024 TC Energy spinoff); Gulf Coast leg design capacity; Reuters, Apr 2024 for the Marketlink figure; PHMSA amended Corrective Action Orders, Mar 2023 and Apr 2025
supply.note: The only single system Hardisty to Houston path, via the Gulf Coast Extension to Nederland and Port Arthur and the Houston Lateral (online 2017). Design capacity is 700.0 kb/d; Reuters cites the Marketlink service at 750.0 kb/d and no South Bow primary source states a Marketlink capacity, so the conflict ships as a range. Mainline nominal capacity is 591.0 kb/d and the system operating capacity routinely cited is 622.0 kb/d, which are different things from the Gulf leg. Effective capacity is below nameplate under PHMSA pressure restrictions imposed after the Dec 2022 Kansas spill and the Apr 2025 Fort Ransom failure, and no public source quantifies the derate or confirms the restrictions have been lifted.

supply.label: Seaway, Cushing to Jones Creek (Freeport) with ECHO lateral
supply.source: Enterprise and Enbridge releases, 2012 to 2014; Argus, Oct 2018; EIA project data via Global Energy Monitor for the drag reducing agent expansion
supply.note: Nameplate carried at 850.0 kb/d (legacy line about 400.0 plus Twin about 450.0). A drag reducing agent expansion to about 950.0 kb/d was announced in 2018 and is recorded as completed in 2019 in EIA project data, but no current operator nameplate was found, so 950.0 is footnoted, not carried. Seaway ends at Jones Creek near Freeport. Houston delivery is a downstream 65 mile lateral to ECHO (Jan 2015) whose capacity is not published, so this is a hub area inbound item, not a metered Houston delivery figure, and the Freeport and Houston split is not quantifiable from public sources. Upstream, Enbridge Flanagan South (in service Dec 2014 at about 600.0 kb/d, designed expandable to about 800.0) plus Spearhead (193.3 kb/d) give about 775.0 to 793.0 kb/d of Flanagan to Cushing capacity behind this line; that upstream steel is not counted again in the inbound total. Slate is whatever sits at Cushing: Canadian heavy via Flanagan South, Bakken, Midcontinent and Permian light.

supply.label: Wink to Webster
supply.source: Oil and Gas Journal, Oct 2020; RBN, Jul 2025 for joint venture stakes
supply.note: 650 miles, 36 inch, 1,500.0 kb/d design for crude and condensate, in service Oct 2020. Origins Wink and Midland; destinations Webster, Baytown and ECHO, with Texas City and Beaumont connectivity. Operated by ExxonMobil in a joint venture with Plains, MPLX, Delek, Lotus (now Energy Transfer) and Rattler (now Diamondback). Permian light sweet and condensate slate. Enterprise's 450.0 kb/d Midland to ECHO 3 interest is an undivided interest in this steel and is counted here, once.

supply.label: Midland to ECHO, M2E-1 distinct steel (Enterprise)
supply.source: Enterprise releases, 2018 to 2019; Enterprise 10-K system figures
supply.note: M2E-1 is Midland to Sealy (416 miles, 24 inch, full service Apr 2018, raised to 620.0 kb/d in Mar 2019) plus Rancho II from Sealy to ECHO. Only the 620.0 kb/d of distinct steel is counted here. Enterprise's Midland to ECHO system total is about 1,070.0 kb/d (620.0 plus the 450.0 kb/d undivided interest in Wink to Webster), and that 450.0 is counted once, inside the Wink to Webster item, not here. M2E-2 (Seminole Red, about 200.0 kb/d in crude service) converted back to natural gas liquids in Dec 2023 and is excluded. M2E-4 was cancelled in Sep 2020. Enterprise publishes no single system capacity figure; the 1,070.0 total is arithmetic on sourced components.

supply.label: BridgeTex to Magellan East Houston (MEH)
supply.note: Colorado City and Midland to ONEOK's East Houston terminal (MEH), about 400 miles, in service Sep 2014. Capacity is 440.0 kb/d from the Plains 2024 10-K. The roughly 560.0 kb/d figure sometimes quoted could not be verified anywhere and is not carried. Ownership per SEC filings is ONEOK via Magellan 30 percent and operator, OMERS 50 percent and Plains 20 percent; a May 2026 Reuters report of about 60 and 40 percent contradicts both companies' filings, and the filings are treated as authoritative. With Longhorn it is the quality controlled unblended Permian feed that underpins MEH pricing.

supply.label: Longhorn to Magellan East Houston (MEH)
supply.note: Crane and Colorado City to MEH at 275.0 kb/d. With BridgeTex it delivers unblended, consistent Midland quality barrels, the property the ICE Midland WTI American Gulf Coast contract design relied on.

supply.label: Enterprise South Texas system (Eagle Ford to ECHO)
supply.note: Eagle Ford origins to Sealy and on to ECHO, including the Eagle Ford pipeline and Rancho connectivity. Current system figure is about 450.0 kb/d of crude and condensate, a system total shared with Rancho connectivity. Do not add the Rancho II Sealy to ECHO segment (over 1,000.0 kb/d) separately; it is shared steel. Phase I was 350.0 kb/d in 2012.

supply.label: Kinder Morgan Crude and Condensate (KMCC) to Houston Ship Channel
supply.note: DeWitt and Gonzales area origins to Houston Ship Channel terminals including Galena Park, 300.0 kb/d, in service Jun 2012. Slate is condensate heavy. Houston bound Eagle Ford nameplate with the Enterprise South Texas item is about 750.0 kb/d. The Plains and Enterprise Eagle Ford joint venture (660.0 kb/d) serves Corpus Christi directly with only a connection option into Houston at Sealy, so it is not counted as Houston inbound.

supply.label: Permian Express to Nederland and Sour Lake (adjacent, not Houston inbound)
supply.source: Energy Transfer FERC Tariff No. 4.21.0, effective Jul 2026; RBN, 2025
supply.note: Memo item, excluded from Houston inbound totals. Energy Transfer's Permian Express is a system of about 600.0 kb/d from Midland to Nederland and Sour Lake, with onward connection to the Houston Ship Channel and HFOTCO. It feeds the Golden Triangle demand block, so it competes for the same Permian barrel rather than supplying Houston proper. There is no pipeline called Midland Express running Permian crude to Houston; that name belongs to an in basin Midland gathering system and to a Phillips 66 natural gas pipeline announced in May 2026.

supply.label: Crude imports into PADD 3, all origins (context series)
supply.source: EIA annual crude import series (PET_MOVE_IMPCP and PADD trade series)
supply.note: Memo item, PADD 3 grain, not a Houston port figure. PADD 3 crude imports from all origins were 1,337.0 kb/d in 2024 and 1,153.0 kb/d in 2025, down from about 5,400.0 to 5,900.0 kb/d in the 2000s. The pipeline systems in this feed are, in aggregate, the replacement supply. A Houston port only import volume is not published in the EIA series retrieved. The heavy end of the waterborne slate is Mexican Maya (Pemex formula priced, not a spot market), Colombian, Ecuadorian and Brazilian heavies and mediums, and medium sour Mars, which competes for coker blendstock rather than grade for grade with WCS.

supply.label: Canadian crude into PADD 3 (context series)
supply.note: Memo item, import area basis, not a Houston metered figure. Canadian crude into PADD 3 was 589.0 kb/d in 2022, 536.0 kb/d in 2023, 526.0 kb/d in 2024 and 416.0 kb/d in 2025. This series counts Canadian barrels however they arrive, overwhelmingly by pipeline at this destination, so it overlaps the capacity items above and is never added to them. The 2025 drop coincides with the first full year of TMX; EIA does not state causation, so the diversion reading is labelled inference. Separate held context: EIA PADD 2 to PADD 3 pipeline receipts were 1,444.0 kb/d in Jul 2026, covering the Keystone, Flanagan and Seaway family.

supply.label: Express, Platte and Capline route to Louisiana (competitor, not Houston inbound)
supply.source: Reuters and Pipeline and Gas Journal, May 2020; CER, Oct 2020; Capline owners announcement, 2017; RBN, Dec 2023
supply.note: Memo item, excluded from Houston inbound totals. Express runs Hardisty to Casper at 280.0 kb/d. Platte runs Casper to Guernsey at 164.0 kb/d and Guernsey to Wood River at 145.0 kb/d, and Wood River and Patoka refining demand takes these barrels first. Capline southbound capacity is about 300.0 kb/d initial (owner announced 2017, in service Dec 2021); the 1,200.0 kb/d figure is the dead northbound nameplate and must not be used, and flows run well below 300.0. Capline lands in Louisiana, so for Houston it is a competitor for the Canadian barrel, and its Express fed ceiling is Platte's 145.0 kb/d Wood River leg in any case.

demand.label: Galveston Bay refinery (Marathon), Texas City
demand.note: Crude distillation capacity 631,000 b/cd exactly, carried here as 631.0 kb/d. Largest metro demand item. Delayed coking 32,500 b/sd plus a resid hydrocracker of 87,000 b/sd, so its heavy conversion sits in the resid hydrocracker, not the small coker. FCC 219,500 b/sd. Formed in 2018 by integrating the former BP Texas City refinery with Marathon's adjacent legacy Texas City plant; there is no separate Marathon Texas City entry in EIA data. After the STAR project (2023) Marathon guided the plant can process significantly more discounted heavy crude (Marathon Q1 2023 earnings call).

demand.label: Baytown refinery (ExxonMobil)
demand.note: Crude distillation capacity 564,500 b/cd exactly, carried here as 564.5 kb/d. Coking is delayed 54,000 b/sd plus fluid coking 42,000 b/sd, total 96,000 b/sd. FCC 220,000 b/sd, vacuum 297,000 b/sd. ExxonMobil's fact sheet calls it a maximum conversion refinery with flexibility for heavy, high sulfur and high metal crudes. The delayed coker was built in 2001 under a Pemex arrangement for Mexican Maya.

demand.label: Deer Park refinery (Pemex)
demand.note: Crude distillation capacity 312,500 b/cd exactly, carried here as 312.5 kb/d. Delayed coking 96,000 b/sd, the largest coker in the metro. FCC 75,100 b/sd. Purpose built heavy plant (the 1990s Shell and Pemex Maya Project, designed around about 140.0 to 160.0 kb/d of heavy crude). Pemex has been sole owner since Jan 20, 2022. Reuters (Feb 2022) reported Pemex agreed to supply it over 100.0 kb/d of Maya, so its coker is both the metro's biggest heavy sink and a captive Maya outlet, which makes WCS the swing heavy barrel at this plant.

demand.label: Valero Texas City refinery
demand.note: Crude distillation capacity 225,000 b/cd exactly, carried here as 225.0 kb/d. Delayed coking 53,500 b/sd. FCC 86,000 b/sd. Valero's 10-K says it processes primarily sour crude oils. The coker was built under a Pemex heavy Maya supply deal (Energy Intelligence, Jan 2002).

demand.label: Valero Houston refinery (Manchester)
demand.note: Crude distillation capacity 205,000 b/cd exactly, carried here as 205.0 kb/d. No coker. FCC 75,200 b/sd and vacuum capacity of only 38,000 b/sd. The least heavy capable large plant in the metro: not a raw heavy buyer, it runs lighter and medium slates and blendstock.

demand.label: Chevron Pasadena refinery
demand.note: Crude distillation capacity 118,750 b/cd exactly, carried here as 118.8 kb/d. No coking and no FCC in the EIA 2026 table. A light plant, not a heavy buyer: bought in 2019 for light crude, and a Dec 2024 retrofit raised light crude processing to about 125,000 b/d on a company basis (Chevron release, Dec 10, 2024). Reuters (Jul 2021) reported the FCC, shut in Jun 2021, was considered for permanent closure toward a hydroskimming configuration; no Chevron statement explicitly confirming permanent FCC removal was found.

demand.label: Petromax refinery, Houston
demand.note: Crude distillation capacity 25,000 b/cd exactly, carried here as 25.0 kb/d. Small topping plant with no conversion.

demand.label: Kinder Morgan Galena Park condensate splitter
demand.note: Condensate splitter capacity 105,000 b/cd exactly, carried here as 105.0 kb/d. Light ends only. Splitters are never heavy demand and are excluded from the core refining nameplate card; they are included in the with splitters card.

demand.label: Hartree Channelview splitter
demand.note: Splitter capacity 45,000 b/cd exactly, carried here as 45.0 kb/d. Light ends only, never heavy demand.

demand.label: Texas International Terminals Galveston splitter
demand.note: Splitter capacity 45,000 b/cd exactly, carried here as 45.0 kb/d. Light ends only, never heavy demand.

demand.label: Crude exports loaded at Houston area terminals
demand.note: Vessel tracking estimates only; there is no EIA port only export series for Houston. Houston area loadings were about 700.0 kb/d in Jul 2022 (Kpler via Reuters) and about 1,020.0 kb/d in Dec 2019 (Petro-Logistics), so the item ships as a range across those two dated observations, not as a current rate. Terminal level loading capability estimates (RBN, 2020, estimates not nameplates) are carried on the terminal items in the storage block: Seaway Texas City about 300.0 kb/d, Seaway Freeport about 200.0 kb/d, Seabrook about 300.0 kb/d and HFOTCO about 480.0 kb/d, plus an Enterprise Houston Ship Channel dock nameplate claimed at over 2,000.0 kb/d in 2018. EIA's Houston Galveston customs district includes Galveston to Corpus Christi by definition and cannot be read as Houston loadings. Corpus Christi took the top US crude export spot in Sep 2019 and held it, at about 2,000.0 kb/d by Jul 2022.

demand.label: Eastbound deliveries from Houston terminals to Beaumont and Port Arthur
demand.source: Enterprise (ECHO to Beaumont and Port Arthur lateral, Dec 2014); ONEOK Houston Distribution System description, accessed Oct 2026
demand.note: ECHO connects to Beaumont and Port Arthur by a roughly 100 mile Enterprise lateral completed in Dec 2014, and the Houston Distribution System reaches refineries further east through third party lines out of MEH. The lateral's capacity is not published in the sources retrieved, so no number is carried. The adjacent complex this item feeds is carried as the five adjacent demand items in this list. Inside the hub, the Houston Distribution System (ONEOK) has capacity above 1,500.0 kb/d linking MEH to Houston and Texas City refineries, to refineries further east and to export terminals including Seabrook, and title transfers at MEH routinely exceed 1,000.0 kb/d. The HoustonLink joint venture (ONEOK and South Bow) moves Canadian, Rockies and Midcontinent crude from South Bow's Houston terminal into MEH. Intra hub plumbing is not counted as an arrival in the supply list.

demand.label: LyondellBasell Houston refinery (permanently closed, memo)
demand.source: LyondellBasell Q1 2025 earnings; EIA Today in Energy, Jun 29, 2026; C&EN, Apr 2022
demand.note: Memo item, excluded from all demand sums because the plant is closed. Capacity at closure was 263,776 b/cd, carried here as 263.8 kb/d. LyondellBasell said it ceased business operations at the Houston refinery in Feb 2025; EIA dates the end of refining operations to Mar 2025, a wind down definition difference. The plant is absent from EIA's Jan 1, 2026 operable list: permanently closed, not idled, and no sale occurred after it was offered from Sep 2021. It was a heavy plant (two cokers of about 42,000 and about 57,000 b/d on Reuters reporting from May 2016, dated figures), so the closure is a permanent loss of heavy demand, the single largest change in the Houston heavy balance in a decade. Any Houston heavy balance built on pre 2025 capacity overstates heavy demand by roughly this plant.

demand.label: Port Arthur refinery (Motiva), adjacent
demand.note: Adjacent item, flagged adjacent and memo, excluded from in hub demand sums. Crude distillation capacity 656,400 b/cd exactly, carried here as 656.4 kb/d, the largest US refinery by calendar day capacity in EIA's 2025 and 2026 reports. Delayed coking 178,000 b/sd, the largest coker in the adjacent block. The 2007 expansion was designed for heavy, sour, acidic crudes as well as bitumen from Canada's oil sands (Energy Intelligence, Sep 2007). A Reuters unit split of about 54,000 plus about 110,000 b/sd sums below the EIA total; the EIA total is carried.

demand.label: Beaumont refinery (ExxonMobil), adjacent
demand.note: Adjacent item, flagged adjacent and memo, excluded from in hub demand sums. Crude distillation capacity 612,000 b/cd exactly, carried here as 612.0 kb/d. Delayed coking 47,000 b/sd. The 2023 expansion (plus 250,000 b/d on a company basis, Mar 2023 release) was a light project fed by Wink to Webster, which dilutes the site's heavy intensity.

demand.label: Valero Port Arthur refinery, adjacent
demand.note: Adjacent item, flagged adjacent and memo, excluded from in hub demand sums. Crude distillation capacity 385,000 b/cd exactly, carried here as 385.0 kb/d. Delayed coking 161,000 b/sd. Deep heavy and sour conversion by explicit design (Valero, Feb 2008). A 2026 trade press figure of 435.0 kb/d of heavy sour throughput exceeds EIA's 385,000 b/cd and 424,000 b/sd for the site and is excluded as irreconcilable.

demand.label: TotalEnergies Port Arthur refinery, adjacent
demand.note: Adjacent item, flagged adjacent and memo, excluded from in hub demand sums. Crude distillation capacity 238,000 b/cd exactly, carried here as 238.0 kb/d. Delayed coking 60,000 b/sd. The 2.2 billion dollar Deep Conversion Project was completed in 2011 for heavy and sour crude.

demand.label: Sweeny refinery (Phillips 66), adjacent
demand.source: EIA Refinery Capacity Report 2026, Table 3 (coking); Merey Sweeny LP SEC filings (coker unit figure)
demand.note: Adjacent item, flagged adjacent and memo, excluded from in hub demand sums. Crude distillation capacity 277,000 b/cd exactly, carried here as 277.0 kb/d. Delayed coking is 78,732 b/sd in EIA, against a 70,000 b/d unit figure in Merey Sweeny LP SEC filings; the basis difference is unresolved and the EIA figure is carried. The plant was built around Venezuelan Merey residue (Merey Sweeny LP, wholly Phillips 66 since Feb 2017), and WCS is its closest quality substitute since Venezuelan supply was impaired.

groups.label: Canada origin barrels
groups.source: Sections 3.1, 3.2, 3.6 and 3.7 of the Houston dossier
groups.note: Value is null because the members carry mixed states: a capacity range on the Keystone Gulf leg, capacity only on Seaway, and a measured PADD 3 import series that overlaps both. The two full paths are Keystone and Marketlink direct to Houston, and Mainline to Flanagan South to Seaway, now anchored at the Enbridge Houston Oil Terminal (see storage). Behind Seaway, Flanagan South plus Spearhead give about 775.0 to 793.0 kb/d into Cushing. Keystone is under PHMSA pressure restrictions with no confirmed restoration, and Mainline apportionment rations the Flanagan and Seaway path in heavy months.

groups.label: Permian origin barrels (distinct steel)
groups.note: Sum of distinct steel nameplates: Wink to Webster 1,500.0 plus M2E-1 620.0 plus BridgeTex 440.0 plus Longhorn 275.0 equals 2,835.0 kb/d. Enterprise's 450.0 kb/d undivided interest in Wink to Webster is counted once, inside Wink to Webster, so the Midland to ECHO system total of about 1,070.0 kb/d is not added on top. Permian Express (about 600.0 kb/d to Nederland) is a memo supply item outside this group because it feeds the adjacent block, not Houston. Houston metro light capable demand is a fraction of this inbound nameplate, so the surplus has to clear at export parity.

groups.label: Eagle Ford origin barrels
groups.note: Enterprise South Texas about 450.0 plus KMCC 300.0 equals 750.0 kb/d of Houston bound Eagle Ford nameplate. Light crude and condensate.

groups.label: Marine imports
groups.note: Value is null at hub grain: the only sourced series is PADD 3 imports (1,153.0 kb/d in 2025, all origins), and no Houston port only or Maya only volume is published in the EIA series retrieved. Houston's import docks are the Seaway Texas City terminal and Enterprise's Houston Ship Channel terminal (see storage).

groups.label: Midcontinent and Bakken share of the Cushing pool (Seaway residual)
groups.note: Value is null. Seaway's slate is whatever sits at Cushing (Canadian heavy via Flanagan South, Bakken, Midcontinent and Permian light) and the split by origin is not published. The non Canadian share can only be backed into from EIA PADD movement series and is not carried as a number.

groups.label: Refineries, heavy capable (in hub)
groups.note: Crude distillation capacity of the four heavy capable metro plants: Galveston Bay 631.0 plus Baytown 564.5 plus Deer Park 312.5 plus Valero Texas City 225.0 equals 1,733.0 kb/d. This is crude capacity at plants with heavy conversion hardware, not heavy crude runs; no public source publishes plant level crude slates or WCS receipts by refinery, and the ranking of these plants as WCS buyers is an inference from conversion hardware plus sourced design and supply statements. The closed LyondellBasell plant is a memo demand item and is not in this group total.

groups.label: Refineries, light and other (in hub)
groups.note: Valero Houston 205.0 plus Chevron Pasadena 118.8 plus Petromax 25.0 equals 348.8 kb/d of crude capacity at plants with no coking. These are not raw heavy buyers.

groups.label: Condensate splitters and small light units (in hub)
groups.note: 105.0 plus 45.0 plus 45.0 equals 195.0 kb/d. Light ends only, never heavy demand. Core metro refining (2,081.8 kb/d) plus this group equals the metro total including splitters (2,276.8 kb/d).

groups.label: Exports by terminal
groups.source: Section 5.1 of the Houston dossier; RBN terminal estimates, 2020
groups.note: Value is null because the only sourced hub total is a range across two dated vessel tracking observations (about 700.0 kb/d in Jul 2022 and about 1,020.0 kb/d in Dec 2019) and the terminal splits are RBN estimates, not nameplates or loadings. Terminal detail is on the storage terminal items. The Houston Ship Channel is maintained at minus 45 feet, which caps loadings at Aframax and part loaded Suezmax economics, with VLCCs only part loaded (about 1,100.0 kb at Texas City) and topped off offshore by reverse lightering. Corpus Christi deepened its channel to 54 feet in Jun 2025. Every crude terminal in Houston is private; Port Houston, the public authority, is a container and general cargo operator.

groups.label: Eastbound and Golden Triangle (adjacent complex)
groups.note: Adjacent refining capacity: 656.4 plus 612.0 plus 385.0 plus 238.0 plus 277.0 equals 2,168.4 kb/d (2,168,400 b/cd). These plants are reachable from Houston terminals by lateral and distribution lines, so they bid on Houston landed barrels. They are flagged adjacent and memo and are excluded from in hub demand sums. Core Houston metro refining (2,081.8 kb/d) plus this block equals about 4,250.2 kb/d of core plants. Argus's Houston area for the WCS Houston assessment explicitly includes Nederland, Beaumont and the ECHO terminal, so this block is inside the pricing footprint even though it is outside the in hub balance.

groups.label: Resid destruction, Houston metro
groups.note: This group is conversion unit capacity in barrels per stream day (b/sd), not barrels per calendar day, and the value is stated in those units even though the field name says kbd. It is coking and resid hydrocracking capacity. It is not coker feed flow and it is not heavy crude runs. Metro delayed coking is 236,000 b/sd (Deer Park 96,000 plus Baytown 54,000 plus Valero Texas City 53,500 plus Galveston Bay 32,500). Baytown fluid coking adds 42,000 b/sd, taking total metro coking to 278,000 b/sd. Galveston Bay's resid hydrocracker adds 87,000 b/sd. Total metro resid destruction is about 365,000 b/sd. This is the scarce hardware in the hub and the denominator of the WCS Houston auction: Argus Consulting estimates US Gulf Coast coking capacity at about 1,700.0 kb/d, more than double the second highest region (China).

groups.label: Resid destruction, adjacent complex
groups.note: Delayed coking capacity in barrels per stream day (b/sd), conversion unit capacity only, not coker feed flow and not heavy crude runs. Motiva Port Arthur 178,000 plus Valero Port Arthur 161,000 plus Sweeny 78,732 plus TotalEnergies Port Arthur 60,000 plus ExxonMobil Beaumont 47,000 equals 524,732 b/sd, carried as 524.7. The adjacent block's two biggest cokers (Motiva 178,000 and Valero Port Arthur 161,000 b/sd) are each larger than any single Houston metro coker.

groups.label: Resid destruction, Houston metro plus adjacent
groups.note: Metro resid destruction of about 365,000 b/sd plus adjacent delayed coking of 524,732 b/sd equals about 889,732 b/sd, carried as 889.7. All figures are conversion unit capacity in barrels per stream day. This group is the heavy lens East Daley's grammar does not carry: heavy demand at this hub is a fixed stock of conversion hardware bidding for a variable supply of discounted heavy barrels, and coker outages and turnarounds move the WCS Houston differential more than crude balances do.

prices.label: WCS Houston differential to WTI calendar month average (CMA)
prices.source: Argus Americas Crude assessment (licensed series, not held); ICE Futures US Rulebook, Subchapter 19C, Rule 19.C.102 for the contract definition
prices.note: No value is carried because the dossier holds no sourced print and the Argus spot assessment is a licensed series that is not held. Do not fabricate one. This is the hub's anchor price: a delivered pipeline spot price for Western Canadian Select (about 20 to 22 degrees API, maximum about 3.5 percent sulfur) in the Houston area, published by Argus as a differential to the NYMEX WTI calendar month average, with an outright price struck off CMA. Argus assesses WCS and Cold Lake transactions together and uses volume weighted average differentials; if the grades diverge, only the more consistently liquid grade's deals are used. The assessment footprint is the point most often got wrong: Argus's location reads Houston area, footnoted as including Nederland, Beaumont and the Enterprise ECHO terminals, so the price is struck over the whole Golden Triangle delivery pool, not the city. The ICE WCS Houston differential future (ARV, 1,000 barrel lots) cash settles on this Argus assessment. Platts also assesses WCS at Cushing and Nederland on CMA bases; its Houston specific specification could not be verified from public sources and Argus's footprint footnote must not be attributed to Platts.

prices.label: WCS Houston premium to a Vancouver high TAN benchmark, 2025 average
prices.source: Pembina Institute, Sep 2026, citing CER proceeding evidence
prices.note: The one sourced relative price the dossier carries: WCS Houston averaged about 1.43 dollars per barrel above a Vancouver high TAN benchmark in 2025. The source is an advocacy organisation citing regulatory filings, and it is carried with that attribution. Canadian netback work treats the Enbridge and Keystone route, not TMX, as the price setting route for WCS.

prices.label: Midland WTI at MEH and ECHO (ICE HOU futures delivery point)
prices.source: ICE Midland WTI American Gulf Coast futures (HOU) contract specification; ICE launch material, 2021 to 2022
prices.note: No value is carried because the dossier holds no sourced print. HOU has traded since Jan 24, 2022 and is physically deliverable at MEH and ECHO at the seller's option. The grade is 40 to 44 degrees API and under 0.2 percent sulfur after ICE's late 2021 tightening, the same WTI Midland grade that entered the Dated Brent basket in 2023. MEH prices America's light oil because of quality control on the Longhorn and BridgeTex barrels, scale of trade (title transfers at MEH routinely exceed 1,000.0 kb/d), optionality through the Houston Distribution System, the bypass of Cushing, and dock access that turns a domestic price into an export netback price. At launch ICE cited over 4,000.0 kb/d of Midland quality inbound pipeline capacity, access to over 14 Houston area ship docks and 60.0 MMbbl of Magellan plus Enterprise storage; a later ICE brochure restates direct inbound Midland connectivity at about 3,000.0 kb/d, so the launch figure is cited with its vintage.

prices.label: Argus WTI Houston differential (CME HTT underlying)
prices.source: Argus WTI Houston assessment (WTI Midland quality at MEH, published since 2015); CME HTT differential futures (since 2016) and HCL physical WTI Houston contract
prices.note: No value is carried because the dossier holds no sourced print and the Argus assessment is a licensed series that is not held. CME's physical WTI Houston contract (HCL) delivers at ECHO, the Enterprise Houston Ship Channel terminal or Genoa Junction. ECHO and MEH transferred Midland WTI between terminals free during the ICE HOU contract's first year and then at 0.10 dollars per barrel, so the two terminals function as one pricing pool.

prices.label: Hardisty to Houston pipeline toll stack (price corridor cost line)
prices.source: tolls.db (held in the WCSB stack) for the Canadian corridors; carrier tariffs as filed
prices.note: No value is carried because the Houston dossier states the toll stack as a corridor input from tolls.db and prints no toll total of its own, and a toll total must not be invented. The route that closes this is a tolls.db pull for the two full paths (Keystone and Marketlink direct, and Mainline to Flanagan South to Seaway) summed leg by leg from filed tariffs. Filed tariffs are published documents, so this is an assembly task, not a research build.

prices.label: Mexican Maya at the US Gulf Coast (competitor heavy grade)
prices.note: No value is carried because Maya is Pemex formula priced, not a spot market price, so there is no spot print to carry. Maya is the benchmark competitor at the heavy end of the Houston slate, together with Colombian, Ecuadorian and Brazilian heavies and mediums and medium sour Mars. Before WCS Houston existed, Canadian heavy at the Coast was priced off Mars, ASCI or the Maya formula; WCS Houston is the first market based heavy price at the Coast (Argus white paper). Phillips 66's published Gulf Coast refining indicator assumes a crude slate of 70 percent WTI MEH, 20 percent WCS Houston and 10 percent Maya (Phillips 66 Market Indicators, Sep 2026), so the heavy end of Coast margin math is quoted in WCS Houston.

storage.source: ICE launch material, 2021 to 2022 (Magellan plus Enterprise Houston distribution systems); terminal figures from company and exchange statements in the dossier
storage.note: Level and percent full are null: EIA publishes working storage capacity by PADD and for Cushing only, and there is no EIA Houston storage series, so no Houston stock level is carried. Capacity carried at 60.0 MMbbl is the combined crude storage in the Magellan (now ONEOK) and Enterprise Houston distribution systems as stated by ICE at the HOU contract launch. ICE also cited a further 90.0 MMbbl connected to those systems, giving about 150.0 MMbbl of total crude storage capacity in the Houston area on a connected system definition; that is an exchange and operator figure, not a survey, and not tankage physically inside Houston. Bottom up, the named hubs in the terminals list (MEH 20.0, ECHO about 8.3 to 9.0, HFOTCO crude about 7.0, Seabrook 3.1, EHOT 2.5 and Seaway system 6.8) sum to about 48.0 MMbbl before Enterprise Houston Ship Channel crude tankage, refinery tankage and small terminals, which is consistent with the 60.0 figure and with 150.0 only on the broad definition. Crude storage does not bind this hub.

terminals.label: Magellan East Houston terminal (MEH)
terminals.note: Inland terminal, marine loading through Houston Distribution System connected docks such as Seabrook. MEH is the pricing point for the hub (see prices). It is the cleanest current terminal storage figure in Houston. ONEOK acquired Magellan in Sep 2023.

terminals.label: ECHO terminal (Enterprise Crude Houston)
terminals.source: Enterprise release, Jul 2019 (8.3 MMbbl); 2018 CFTC and NYMEX filing (8.0 MMbbl); RBN, 2025 (about 9.0 MMbbl)
terminals.note: Storage ships as a range because no current single ECHO only figure is published. No dock of its own; it loads through the Enterprise Houston Ship Channel terminal. Aggregation hub for Midland to ECHO, Wink to Webster, the Seaway lateral and the Eagle Ford system, and a delivery point for the ICE Midland WTI American Gulf Coast contract at the seller's option.

terminals.label: Enterprise Houston Ship Channel terminal (EHSC, including former Oiltanking Houston)
terminals.source: 2018 filing (about 23 MMbbl); Argus, 2022 (about 27 MMbbl, all products)
terminals.note: Storage is all products; the crude only split is not published, so the figure ships as a range and is not added to crude storage totals. Seven deepwater ship docks, draft to 45 feet, Suezmax capable, tankers to about 900 kb per the 2018 filing. Oiltanking Houston and Beaumont were acquired with Oiltanking Partners in Oct 2014 (about 24 MMbbl combined, no Houston only split). Enterprise executives claimed over 2,000.0 kb/d of crude export dock capacity at Houston in 2018; that is a dock nameplate claim, not a loading rate.

terminals.label: Seaway Texas City and Freeport (Jones Creek) terminals
terminals.source: Seaway joint venture system figures; RBN, 2020 for export capability estimates
terminals.note: System Gulf Coast tankage is 6.8 MMbbl, of which Jones Creek is 2.8 MMbbl; a Texas City only storage figure is not published, so the system figure is carried and labelled as such. Texas City has 2 docks, 45 foot draft and 35,000 barrels per hour, and hosted the first partial VLCC loadings at a Texas port in 2018 (about 1,100.0 kb loaded, topped off by offshore lightering). RBN estimated export capacity at about 300.0 kb/d for Texas City and about 200.0 kb/d for Freeport in 2020; those are estimates, not nameplates. The Texas City distribution system moves waterborne barrels from the marine dock into Texas City and Houston refineries and is separate from the Cushing line's capacity.

terminals.label: Houston Fuel Oil Terminal (HFOTCO)
terminals.source: Energy Transfer release, 2019 (over 18 MMbbl, labelled crude); RBN, 2020 (split of about 7 MMbbl crude and about 11 MMbbl residual fuel oil)
terminals.note: Total storage is about 18.0 MMbbl. The crude share is carried at about 7.0 MMbbl on RBN's 2020 split because the primary business is residual fuel oil; Energy Transfer's own 2019 release labels the full 18.0 MMbbl as crude, and that conflict is recorded here rather than resolved. Five deepwater ship docks plus seven barge docks, Suezmax at 45 foot draft. RBN estimated export capability at about 480.0 kb/d (2020 estimate). The 75 mile Ted Collins line connects HFOTCO to Energy Transfer's Nederland terminal (about 500.0 kb/d, announced 2019).

terminals.label: Seabrook Logistics terminal
terminals.source: Magellan and LBC expansion release, 2018; RBN, 2020 for the export estimate
terminals.note: Storage about 3.1 MMbbl after the 2018 expansion. Aframax and Suezmax docks at 45 foot draft, with about 400.0 kb/d of dock capacity from the 2018 expansion. RBN estimated export capability at about 300.0 kb/d in 2020. Seabrook is the Houston Distribution System's export outlet.

terminals.label: Enbridge Houston Oil Terminal (EHOT), Jones Creek
terminals.source: Enbridge releases, Jul 2026 and in service reporting
terminals.note: Initial storage 2.5 MMbbl in four tanks. Enbridge releases also state 2.7 MMbbl (four tanks at 680 kb each is 2.72 MMbbl); 2.5 is carried as the in service shell figure and the conflict is recorded. Ultimate potential is about 15.0 MMbbl. Dock loading runs through Seaway Freeport and Texas City. In service in the first half of 2026. It is a greenfield heavy terminal fed on the full Mainline to Flanagan South to Seaway path and is the newest piece of Houston heavy infrastructure, and the only recent Houston heavy addition is a terminal, not conversion capacity.

terminals.label: Kinder Morgan Ship Channel and Galena Park terminals
terminals.note: Storage is 43.0 MMbbl of all liquids on a 2015 vintage, which is not a crude figure, so no crude storage number is carried for this terminal. Its Houston crude relevance is the Galena Park condensate splitter (a demand item in this feed) and inbound connectivity, not export docks.

corridors.label: Hardisty to Houston, Keystone and Marketlink direct
corridors.note: The only single system Hardisty to Houston path, over the Gulf Coast Extension to Nederland and Port Arthur with the Houston Lateral branching to Houston area refineries and terminals. Owner is South Bow. Runs under PHMSA pressure restrictions with no confirmed restoration date. HoustonLink then bridges South Bow's Houston terminal into MEH.

corridors.label: Hardisty to Cushing to Houston area, Mainline, Flanagan South and Seaway
corridors.to: Jones Creek (Freeport), ECHO and Houston area terminals
corridors.note: Mainline to Flanagan South (about 600.0 kb/d at sanction, expandable to about 800.0) plus Spearhead (193.3 kb/d) give about 775.0 to 793.0 kb/d into Cushing, then Seaway (850.0 kb/d carried) to Jones Creek, then an unpublished capacity lateral to ECHO and onward to Beaumont and Port Arthur. The Enbridge Houston Oil Terminal at Jones Creek is fed on this full path. Midwest refineries bid for the same barrels before they reach Cushing, and Mainline apportionment rations this path in heavy months.

corridors.label: Permian to Houston, MEH and ECHO pricing pool
corridors.to: MEH, ECHO, Webster, Baytown and Texas City
corridors.note: 2,835.0 kb/d of distinct steel nameplate. This corridor is why MEH is a pricing point: unblended Midland quality barrels from BridgeTex and Longhorn, plus Wink to Webster and Midland to ECHO volume, reaching refineries and export docks from one pool without touching Cushing.

corridors.label: Eagle Ford to Houston
corridors.to: ECHO and Houston Ship Channel terminals
corridors.note: About 750.0 kb/d of Houston bound nameplate. Competing Eagle Ford and Permian systems (Cactus II at 670.0 kb/d and Harvest) run to Corpus Christi and Ingleside, not Houston.

corridors.label: Houston terminals to the Golden Triangle (eastbound)
corridors.to: Beaumont, Port Arthur and Sweeny, Texas
corridors.note: The adjacent complex (2,168.4 kb/d of distillation and 524,732 b/sd of delayed coking) bids directly on Houston landed barrels, and Argus's WCS Houston footprint already includes Nederland and Beaumont. The ECHO to Beaumont and Port Arthur lateral's capacity is not published.

corridors.label: WCS Houston price corridor, Hardisty to Houston
corridors.to: Houston area (Argus footprint: Nederland, Beaumont and ECHO included)
corridors.note: Price legs: the WCS Houston differential to CMA (Argus assessment, ICE ARV settles on it), Midland WTI at MEH and ECHO as the hub flat price point, and the Hardisty to Houston toll stack from tolls.db as the cost line. All three are carried in the prices list; none carries an invented value. See the prices entries wcs_houston_diff_cma, wti_meh_hou and hardisty_houston_toll_stack.

corridors.label: Competing corridors for the Canadian barrel (Capline to Louisiana, TMX to Westridge)
corridors.to: St. James, Louisiana, and Westridge (Burnaby), British Columbia
corridors.note: Neither competing corridor feeds Houston. Capline lands Canadian barrels in Louisiana at about 300.0 kb/d of southbound capacity, bottlenecked by Platte's 145.0 kb/d Wood River leg on the Express fed path. TMX (890.0 kb/d to Westridge, in service May 1, 2024, Aframax only with partial cargoes of about 550.0 to 600.0 kb) competes for the same barrel and is taking the marginal one: over 65 percent of Westridge exports go to Asia (Trans Mountain CEO, APPEC Sep 2026), Canadian exports to non US destinations rose from near zero to about 430.0 kb/d in 2025, China bound shipments via US Gulf Coast terminals fell to zero after TMX (Kpler via Oil Sands Magazine, Dec 2025), and Canadian crude into PADD 3 fell from 589.0 kb/d in 2022 to 416.0 kb/d in 2025. Before TMX about 200.0 kb/d of western Canadian crude was re exported out of the US Gulf Coast (Vortexa, 2023). No regular TMX to Houston cargo programme was found in any source. The TMX diversion reading of the PADD 3 series is inference, not an EIA statement.

notes: Houston is a demand and pricing hub, not a production hub. In this feed, supply means barrels that arrive (inbound pipelines and imports) and demand means refineries, export loadings and barrels passed onward east. In region production is not framed by the dossier, so in_region_production_kbd is null rather than zero.

Card convention. nameplate_kbd is the core Houston metro refining nameplate: seven crude refineries totalling 2,081,750 b/cd, carried as 2,081.8 kb/d. It is not the inbound pipeline total and not the metro total with splitters. The other nameplates are carried as separate cards so nothing is double read: inbound_nameplate_kbd 5,135.0 is distinct inbound pipeline steel; refining_nameplate_with_splitters_kbd 2,276.8 adds the three splitter and small units (195.0); adjacent_refining_nameplate_kbd 2,168.4 is the Beaumont, Port Arthur and Sweeny block; hub_plus_adjacent_refining_nameplate_kbd 4,250.2 is core metro plus adjacent (2,081,750 plus 2,168,400 equals 4,250,150 b/cd). resid_destruction_metro_kbd, coking_metro_kbd and coking_adjacent_kbd are conversion unit capacities in barrels per stream day, not calendar day volumes (see the Resid destruction groups).

Cards that are null, and why. supply_kbd is null because no published series gives arrivals into Houston at hub grain and the non memo supply items are capacities and one capacity range, so there is no flow sum to foot. demand_kbd is null for the same reason on the demand side: the non memo demand items are refinery and splitter capacities, one export loadings range and one eastbound item with unpublished capacity. effective_kbd is null because the dossier supports only a range for effective metro crude runs, about 1,900.0 to 2,000.0 kb/d against the 2,081.8 kb/d core nameplate, derived from Texas Gulf Coast district utilization of 91.9 percent in 2025 and PADD 3 utilization of 96.7 percent in Jul 2026; a single point would be invented. exports_kbd is null because Houston loadings ship as a range (700.0 to 1,020.0 kb/d across two dated vessel tracking observations). balance_kbd is null because neither side has a hub grain flow total. in_region_demand_kbd is null because plant level runs are not published, so in hub demand cannot be separated from capacity.

imports_kbd is 1,153.0 kb/d of crude imports into PADD 3 from all origins in 2025, and canadian_imports_padd3_kbd is the Canadian subset at 416.0 kb/d in 2025. Both are PADD grain context series carried on memo supply items. Neither is a Houston port figure, and neither is added to the pipeline capacity items. padd2_to_padd3_pipeline_receipts_kbd is 1,444.0 kb/d for Jul 2026 from the held EIA PADD movement series; it covers the Keystone, Flanagan and Seaway family at PADD grain.

Inbound nameplate footing. inbound_nameplate_kbd 5,135.0 is the sum of distinct steel nameplates on the non memo supply items, using the design figure where an item ships as a range and the distinct steel figure where a system total double counts: Keystone Gulf leg 700.0 (not the 750.0 Marketlink citation) plus Seaway 850.0 (not the 950.0 post expansion figure) plus Wink to Webster 1,500.0 plus Midland to ECHO distinct steel 620.0 (not the 1,070.0 system total, whose 450.0 balance is an undivided interest in Wink to Webster and is counted there) plus BridgeTex 440.0 plus Longhorn 275.0 plus Enterprise South Texas 450.0 plus KMCC 300.0 equals 5,135.0 kb/d, which is the dossier's roughly 5.14 MMb/d of distinct steel. Memo supply items (Permian Express, Capline route, and the two PADD import series) are excluded from that sum.

Demand footing. The seven core refinery items sum to 2,081.8 kb/d of nameplate (631.0 plus 564.5 plus 312.5 plus 225.0 plus 205.0 plus 118.8 plus 25.0), footing to nameplate_kbd within rounding of the exact 2,081,750 b/cd. Adding the three splitter items (195.0) gives 2,276.8 kb/d, footing to refining_nameplate_with_splitters_kbd against the exact 2,276,750 b/cd. The five adjacent items sum to 2,168.4 kb/d, footing exactly to adjacent_refining_nameplate_kbd and to the exact 2,168,400 b/cd. Refinery item values are capacities (state capacity_only, value_kbd null), so these footings are nameplate footings, not flow footings, and demand_kbd stays null.

Adjacent convention. The Beaumont, Port Arthur and Sweeny plants are carried as demand items flagged adjacent and memo. They are excluded from every in hub sum in this feed. They are carried at all because they are reachable from Houston terminals by lateral and distribution lines and bid on Houston landed barrels, and because Argus's Houston area for the WCS Houston assessment explicitly includes Nederland, Beaumont and the Enterprise ECHO terminals. Stated plainly: outside the in hub balance, inside the pricing footprint.

Demand in this feed means cleared flow, not wants or nominations. Refinery demand items are capacities because plant level runs are not published; the flow statement the dossier supports is district level (Texas Gulf Coast utilization 91.9 percent in 2025, PADD 3 96.7 percent in Jul 2026) plus dated export loading observations. No refinery crude slate or nominations figure is presented anywhere in this feed as demand.

Resid destruction is conversion unit capacity, in barrels per stream day. Metro delayed coking of 236,000 b/sd plus Baytown fluid coking of 42,000 b/sd is 278,000 b/sd of metro coking; adding Galveston Bay's 87,000 b/sd resid hydrocracker gives about 365,000 b/sd of metro resid destruction. It is not coker feed flow and it is not heavy crude runs, and it must never be added to calendar day distillation capacity. The adjacent block adds 524,732 b/sd of delayed coking, more than double the metro coking total.

The LyondellBasell Houston refinery (263,776 b/cd) permanently closed in Feb to Mar 2025 and is absent from EIA's Jan 1, 2026 operable list. It is carried as a memo demand item and in the notes only, never in a sum. It was a heavy plant, so the closure removed heavy demand, and any Houston heavy balance built on pre 2025 capacity overstates heavy demand by roughly a quarter million barrels a day of crude capacity.

Corrections that must survive. Keystone's owner is South Bow, not TC Energy (spinoff effective Oct 1, 2024). No pipeline called Midland Express carries Permian crude to Houston. BridgeTex capacity is 440.0 kb/d from Plains' 2024 10-K, not about 560.0. Capline southbound capacity is about 300.0 kb/d, not the dead 1,200.0 kb/d northbound nameplate, and Capline lands in Louisiana. Midland to ECHO is an Enterprise system; no Sunoco or Energy Transfer asset carries that name. Seaway's nameplate ends at Jones Creek (Freeport), and its Houston delivery is a downstream lateral of unpublished capacity. Wink to Webster entered service in Oct 2020, not 2023.

Do not mix EIA products. Texas Gulf Coast district capacity of 5,375 thousand b/cd (2025) comes from EIA's Refinery Utilization and Capacity series, not the Refinery Capacity Report, and the two products use slightly different conventions. The district figure is used in this feed only for utilization context (utilization_pct 91.9 is the Texas Gulf Coast district 2025 average, with PADD 3 at 93.3 percent in 2025 and 96.7 percent in Jul 2026) and is never summed with Capacity Report plant figures. EIA's Houston Galveston customs district likewise includes Galveston to Corpus Christi and cannot be read as Houston port trade.

Slate context. Texas Gulf Coast refinery inputs averaged 35.18 degrees API and 1.48 percent sulfur in 2025 (2024: 34.21 degrees and 1.53 percent), against PADD 3 at 34.63 degrees API and 1.29 percent sulfur (EIA Refinery Crude Oil Input Qualities, release Sep 30, 2026). The Texas coast runs lighter than the PADD average and more sour: a barbelled slate of light shale at one end and heavy sour at the other. WCS competes at the heavy end against Maya and Latin American grades, never against the light end.

What binds this hub is heavy conversion hardware and dock space, not distillation, storage or inbound light pipeline capacity, all of which are in surplus. The Houston Ship Channel is maintained at minus 45 feet, so Houston loadings are Aframax and part loaded Suezmax economics with VLCCs part loaded and topped off offshore, while Corpus Christi loads at 54 feet (deepened Jun 2025). That draft wall is a per barrel cost on every Houston export cargo.

Intra hub plumbing is not supply. The Houston Distribution System (over 1,500.0 kb/d), HoustonLink, and ECHO to MEH transfers move barrels that have already arrived, so they are described on the eastbound demand item and in the corridors, and are never itemized as arrivals. Title transfers at MEH routinely exceed 1,000.0 kb/d (ONEOK).

TMX does not feed Houston. No regular TMX to Houston cargo programme was found in any source. TMX competes with the Houston route for the same Canadian barrel, and the reading that it caused the 2024 to 2025 fall in Canadian crude into PADD 3 (526.0 to 416.0 kb/d) is inference, not an EIA statement, and is labelled as inference wherever it appears in this feed.

gaps.route: A current Enterprise or Enbridge system fact sheet stating Seaway nameplate capacity.

gaps.reason: The Jones Creek to ECHO lateral capacity and the Freeport versus Houston delivery split are not published anywhere, so Seaway cannot be split into Houston and Freeport deliveries from public data.
gaps.route: Carrier tariff or Form 6 delivery point detail for the Seaway joint venture filers; failing that, the split must be modelled and labelled as modelled.

gaps.reason: Flanagan South's current rating is about 600.0 kb/d at sanction against about 800.0 kb/d design expansion; a 2025 trade summary implies the expansion is substantially taken up but no current Enbridge primary document pins it. Combined Flanagan to Cushing is carried in notes at 775.0 to 793.0 kb/d.

Plant level crude slates and WCS receipts by refinery are not public, which is the same hole East Daley acknowledged for Canada.
gaps.route: EIA district grain runs (Texas Gulf Coast utilization, held) allocated to plants only as labelled estimates; plant slates would need company disclosure.

gaps.reason: No published series gives arrivals into Houston at hub grain. Permian and Eagle Ford arrivals into Houston specifically are not published, and pipeline items are capacities, not flows.

gaps.reason: Houston port only crude exports and imports are not published by EIA; the Houston Galveston customs district includes Corpus Christi, and port splits rest on vessel tracking estimates (Kpler, Petro-Logistics, ClipperData). Corpus and Houston share percentages in 2025 trade coverage are attributed to EIA only through secondary republication and are not verified to an EIA table.

gaps.route: An Enterprise terminal fact sheet with a crude only tankage split.

gaps.reason: Total storage of about 18.0 MMbbl is solid but the crude share conflicts: Energy Transfer's release labels it all crude, RBN splits it about 7.0 MMbbl crude and about 11.0 MMbbl residual fuel oil.

gaps.reason: ECHO storage is 8.0 MMbbl in a 2018 filing, 8.3 MMbbl in Enterprise's Jul 2019 release and about 9.0 MMbbl in RBN 2025, with no current single ECHO only figure published.

gaps.reason: Enbridge's own releases state both 2.5 and 2.7 MMbbl for the initial four tanks.
gaps.route: Enbridge's in service terminal fact sheet for EHOT shell capacity.

gaps.reason: There is no EIA Houston storage series and the roughly 150.0 MMbbl Houston area total is an ICE and operator figure from 2021 to 2022 on a connected system definition, not a survey.
gaps.route: Bottom up terminal tankage from company statements (done in this feed) plus AIS and draft observation for levels; no public survey route exists.

gaps.reason: The ECHO to Beaumont and Port Arthur lateral's capacity is not published in the sources retrieved, so eastbound flow out of the Houston balance cannot be sized.
